title: In Step with Belgrade: Pale and the Invincible Package
source_note: The listed adjudicative and institutional sources bound the chronology, actors, and findings described. The essay is original synthesis and does not extend individual liability, command responsibility, or institutional findings beyond the cited record.
content:
In the late summer of 1993 the Bosnian Serb leadership was saying yes. On 28 August the Bosnian Serb Assembly accepted the Geneva accord without conditions. In the same month the VRS pulled back from Igman and Bjelašnica, the mountains above Sarajevo, after the UN and NATO threatened air strikes. On 20 September, aboard the British carrier HMS Invincible, Owen and Stoltenberg put a package to the parties, and Milošević sat at the table. The package gave 49 percent of Bosnia to the Serb republic. Sarajevo would stay undivided, under UN administration for two years.

Belgrade's part that autumn was support. The Karadžić trial judgment shows Milošević backing the Pale leadership in this period, and it does not show him holding Pale back. The strain on the Bosnian Serb leadership that September came from inside. In Banja Luka a mutiny broke out over war profiteering. The mutineers wanted action against the profiteers. The mutiny was settled on 16 September. It was not a revolt against Belgrade.

The package then stalled in the assemblies. On 29 September the Bosnian Assembly accepted it only with conditions. On 1 October the Croat Assembly withdrew the concessions it had offered the Muslims. On 2 October the Bosnian Serb Assembly did the same. Through those weeks Pale and Belgrade moved together. Staying in step with Belgrade was the documented line of autumn 1993.

Open defiance of Belgrade belongs to other seasons. In May 1993 Pale turned down the Vance-Owen plan, which Milošević had pressed it to accept. In July and August 1994 Pale rejected the Contact Group map, and the rift with Belgrade came into the open. The autumn of 1993 lay between those two breaks. For a few weeks Belgrade and the Bosnian Serb leadership held one line. The package stalled all the same, and the war went into its second winter.
